title: Sìleas counts the coal's colours
summary: At the far-eastern Muileann chiar, Sìleas nic Coinnich begins counting which strokes of her own pick break the vein bright with colour and which break it plain dull coal, and notices the bright breaks come to no cutter's hand alone, not even her own, on every shift.

title: Sìleas's mother warns against the asking
summary: Sìleas's mother, who cut the same wall before her, tells her that a question put to the vein is better left unput, and that the mountain has fed the house four generations without being asked why. Sìleas holds her tongue, but not her counting.

title: Sìleas moved from wall to wall
summary: The overseer of Muileann chiar's galleries, wearying of a cutter who tries the coal's answer against fasting, singing and the hour of the day, moves Sìleas nic Coinnich from wall to wall until no face is left that has not already been asked her questions.

title: Sìleas withdraws to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
summary: Sìleas nic Coinnich goes up into Coille Naomh Muileann chiar meaning only to sit and think, and finds three cutters of her own galleries have followed her there unasked, each carrying the same unspoken question from the face.

title: Forty gather in the clearing
summary: Two springs after the first evening in the wood, near forty cutters, basket-carriers and children of the overseer's own house sit in the clearing above Muileann chiar to hear Sìleas nic Coinnich set out her counting, more than the old fallen trunk she taught from can seat.

title: A hearer walks a fortnight to the wood
summary: A woman of the northern shore, having heard a story of a stag grown taller with every telling between her home and the wood, walks a fortnight to sit in Sìleas's clearing, and is told plainly that the counting, not the stag, is the whole of what is taught there.

title: Ìomhar Dearg killed at the ford
summary: Riding to see a moved boundary stone on an Earrann Dhearg's northern march, Ìomhar Dearg is speared through the throat at the ford of the Abhainn dhomhain by Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh, in payment for Aonghas Bàn's death at Dùn thais sixty years before. His riders bring him from the water dead.

title: An Earrann Dhearg held whole under Dùghall Dearg
summary: Dùghall Dearg mac Ìomhair takes up an Earrann Dhearg entire the week his father is buried, and tells the four lines who come to Dùn dhearg with old claims that the share was won with a sword and will be kept with one. None presses a claim against his household.

title: Eachann Ruadh flees to Talla na Lasrach's ground
summary: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh rides through the night from the ford to the ground before Talla na Lasrach, throws down his second spear, and sits within sight of Brìde's fire until Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's cutters come out to him, asking the ground and nothing of the flame itself.

title: Gormshuil rules Talla na Lasrach's ground holds even a killer
summary: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich rules that no spear may follow Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh past Talla na Lasrach's boundary stone, though what waits for him beyond it is not hers to answer for, and lets him raise a hut at the ground's edge to cut turf for Talla na Lasrach's own fires.

title: A loaned cutter's report reaches Gormshuil
summary: A cutter of Dùn ìseal's own galleries, home from a season's loan to Muileann chiar, tells Talla na Lasrach in passing that the eastern cutters count their strokes and ask why the coal answers one hand and not another. Gormshuil sends her own cutter east to see the wood for herself.

title: Sìleas summoned to Dùn ìseal
summary: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich summons Sìleas nic Coinnich to Dùn ìseal, and the two speak alone in the keepers' hut by the flame Beathag Bhàn once held. Neither afterwards gives a full account of what passed between them; only the ruling that follows is known.

title: The eastern cutters walk further into the hills
summary: After the galleries of Dùn ìseal are shut to them, a dozen of Sìleas nic Coinnich's oldest hearers walk east out of Muileann chiar to raise a house of their own further from the mountain's shadow, following the wood where it thickens and the seam where it runs deeper.
